LESSON 6 OF 106·Cyber Security Fundamentals

Security Controls

A control names the risk it reduces. Prevent, detect, correct — you want one of each, not three of the first.

Foundation3 min
Why this matters

A control is a specific thing you do that reduces a specific risk. If you cannot say which risk it reduces, it is not a control — it is a purchase.

What you'll learn

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • classify a control as preventing, detecting or correcting
  • recognise the difference between administrative, technical and physical controls
  • check whether your controls cover all three stages or repeat one

In plain English

A control is an action, not a product. "Turn on full-disk encryption" is a control. "Buy a security suite" is a purchase, and may or may not contain one.

Controls are usually sorted two ways: by what they do, and by what kind of thing they are. Both sorts are useful, and neither is complicated.

How it works

By what they do, there are three stages, and you want at least one control at each:

  • Prevent: stop it happening. Encryption, access rules, patching, a lock.
  • Detect: find out it happened, or is happening. Logs, alerts, a monthly permission review.
  • Correct: recover and learn. Restore from backup, revoke a session, rotate a key, write down what went wrong.

By what kind of thing they are, there are three types, and you want all three too:

  • Administrative: a rule or a habit — "no shared admin accounts".
  • Technical: something the system enforces — permissions, MFA, rate limits.
  • Physical: something in the world — a door code, a locked cabinet, a screen in an office.

The two sorts cross over. A door code is a physical, preventive control. An audit log is a technical, detective control. Neither sorting is better; together they stop you from repeating the same kind of fix.

A worked example

A laptop gets stolen from a café. One risk, three stages, three controls:

  • Prevent: full-disk encryption, so the disk is useless without the login; an automatic screen lock, so the machine is not simply open.
  • Detect: a sign-in alert for a location you have never visited; the ability to see when the device last reported in.
  • Correct: a remote wipe, and a backup that lets you rebuild the machine without paying anything.

Now the three types for the same risk: a policy that laptops may not be left unattended (administrative), encryption and remote wipe (technical), and keeping the bag on your body (physical). Every one of those is cheap, and together they cover the whole event rather than just the moment of theft.

The mistake most beginners make

Stacking the same stage. Two antivirus products, or three password policies, all doing prevention — while nothing anywhere detects a compromise or makes recovery possible. Coverage across the three stages beats depth in one.

The second mistake is a control that nobody verifies. A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a control. The test is the control.

Try it in two minutes

Take one risk you already know about — a stolen phone is a good one — and write three lines:

  • Prevent: what stops this working?
  • Detect: how would I find out in the first hour?
  • Correct: how do I recover without losing more?

If any line is blank, that is where the next hour of effort goes. It is almost never where people start.

Practice / apply

Pick one risk you already know about and write one control for each stage: prevent, detect, correct.

Key takeaways

  • A control names the risk it reduces; a purchase does not.
  • Prevent, detect, correct — you want one of each, not three of the first.
  • Administrative, technical and physical controls cover different failure modes.
  • An untested control is a hope. The test is the control.
